I'm trying to determine whether I would be able to see the Moon right now.

I'm in Quito, Ecuador at 2026-10-18 13:17 -05 (UTC-0500) (2026-10-18T18:17:00Z in UTC), at latitude -0.1807 degrees and longitude -78.4678 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 68.338 degrees and its azimuth is 243.003 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 12.202 degrees and its azimuth is 114.138 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 50.95 percent illuminated, 90.942 degrees from the Sun, and 401155.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably yes, but it would be challenging.

At that time the Moon is about half illuminated and only about 12° above the eastern-southeastern horizon (azimuth ~114°), while the Sun is high in the southwest. A half Moon at roughly 91° elongation from the Sun can be visible in clear daytime sky, especially at Quito’s high elevation and with a clean, dry-looking sky.

The main difficulty is contrast: at 12° altitude, atmospheric haze, buildings, terrain, and glare can substantially reduce visibility. It will not look dramatic; expect a faint, pale semicircular patch rather than a bright nighttime Moon.

To maximize your chances:

- Find an unobstructed view toward azimuth 114° — roughly east-southeast.
- Look about 12° above the true horizon: a little more than one fist held at arm’s length.
- Use the Moon’s expected half-lit shape and scan slowly; do not stare near the Sun.
- If you have binoculars, they can help locate it, but never point them anywhere near the Sun.

With the stated clear sky and accurate position, a person who knows where to look has a good chance of spotting it, though it may take a few minutes of careful searching.
